title: Tenant credit siphon and steadyback: autoscale & isolation sketch
content:
Purpose
This is a sketch for a complementary mechanism to existing reserved + burst flows: the "credit siphon" (temporary micro-credit transfer) paired with a "steadyback" decay rule. The goal is to reduce request-level aborts for short, high-value microbursts while preserving tenant isolation and predictable economics. This doc lays out intent, APIs, accounting, SLO implications, operator signals, and a lightweight rollout path.

Background & problem statement
We repeatedly see short bursts (10s-2m) from tenants that temporarily exceed their committed capacity but represent high-value traffic (e.g., interactive product demos, retraining of a small queue). Current options:
- Hard throttle: fast, predictable, but loses short revenue spikes and hurts UX.
- Admit via opportunistic oversubscription: can give latency regressions to neighbors.
- Manual burst credits: works but is clunky, slow to provision, and rarely used.

We want a mechanism that:
1) lets a tenant absorb a small transient overage without long-term commitment,
2) enforces limits so noisy neighbors are protected,
3) charges an explicit economic signal and decays automatically, and
4) integrates with autoscaling and fallback routing.

Design goals
- Bounded: maximum siphon budget per tenant per epoch (configurable).
- Short-lived: siphoned credits decay via steadyback schedule to avoid permanent debt.
- Observable: full ledger of siphon events for billing/ops and per-request traces for postmortem.
- Deterministic fallback: when siphon exhausted, the request follows the standard fallback ladder (burst pool, lower-fidelity model, reject).
- Admin controls: tenant-level enable/disable, hard caps, and emergency quarantine.

Core concepts
- Micro-credit: a short-lived unit (M-credits) representing compute tokens roughly pegged to token-cost at 100-token granularity.
- Siphon window: sliding 60s window during which tenant is eligible for siphon top-up when committed capacity is saturated.
- Steadyback: exponential-ish decay schedule that returns siphoned allowances to baseline; ensures no long tails. Example: 50% decay each 5 minutes (configurable).
- Siphon ledger entry: immutable record of {time, amount, reason, route, caller-id} for audit. (We store as structured logs; link ids emitted to tracing.)

High-level flow
1) Request arrives and is denied by the tenant's committed pool due to concurrency or token-rate limit.
2) Router evaluates: is tenant allowed siphon? checks hard cap, epoch consumption, and quarantine status.
3) If allowed, router atomically assigns micro-credits from the global siphon namespace for that tenant and routes request to serving runtime.
4) Usage is emitted to the ledger; billing subsystem later converts M-credits to invoice lines with a multiplier.
5) Steadyback policy reduces available siphon budget over time; if tenant resumes normal rate, budget naturally decays.

Autoscaler interactions
- Signal for scale-up: repeated siphon consumption > threshold (e.g., avg siphon > 20% of committed) triggers predictive autoscaler to warm extra dedicated slots for that tenant.
- Signal for don’t scale: one-off siphons under a short window should NOT trigger sustained capacity allocation. Short bursts must be discriminated from workload shifts.
- Backstop: if autoscaler cannot provision in time, siphon acts as a graceful buffer; however we must cap overall latency exposure.

Isolation & safety controls
- Global and tenant hard caps: operator-set ceilings to bound systemic risk.
- Per-route fidelity lanes: siphon can be restricted to certain routes (e.g., low-risk evaluation routes) to avoid premium models being consumed.
- Priority vector: combine tenant tier + route sensitivity to compute siphon eligibility.
- Emergency quarantine: ops can flip a tenant into "siphon-disabled" which also forcibly drains ephemeral credits to zero for next-scheduled decay tick.

Economics and billing
- M-credit pricing: small premium over committed unit price to discourage routine use (e.g., 1.6x committed per-M-credit).
- Ledger -> invoice pipeline: siphon ledger periodically summarized to line-items with tags (siphon, steadyback decay, applied discount credits).
- Cost transparency in Console: per-tenant curve of siphon vs committed spend with tooltipable examples.

APIs and admin UI
- Public API additions: 
  - GET /tenants/{id}/siphon-status -> returns remaining M-credits & decay params
  - POST /tenants/{id}/siphon-override {amount, ttl, reason} (admin only)
  - Streaming traces include siphon id header for per-request correlation
- Console: a compact view in Dedicated -> Tenant -> Capacity showing a small time-series widget for siphon usage and a toggle for enable/disable and hard cap setting.

Telemetry and SLOs
- Primary metrics: siphon_consumed_per_epoch, siphon_requests_ratio, siphon_failure_rate, average_siphon_latency_add.
- SLOs: siphon_handling_latency p95 < 3ms at router level; siphon-accounting correctness 100% (ledger must match traces within 30s).
- Alerting: sustained siphon consumption > 30% of committed for 10m -> Prod alert; mismatched ledger entries -> Payment ops alert.

Operator runbook (initial ops-facing procedures)
- When an alert fires for sustained siphon consumption: check tenant dashboard for route-level spikes -> if legitimate, consider offering a temporary commit; else flip to siphon-disabled and contact account execs.
- If ledger mismatches: enable debug logging, mark time range, collect traces via siphon ids, escalate to infra-payments.
- Emergency: a global "drain-siphons" feature to zero all ephemeral credits for X minutes to protect platform from runaway consumption.

Tradeoffs & alternatives considered
- Simpler per-tenant burst window deposit: too coarse and requires manual top-ups.
- Pure price-signal: letting price alone throttle (spike penalties) risks user surprise and time-to-react mismatch.
- Token-bucket per-route: good isolation but complex to reconcile with billing and autoscaler signals.

Migration & rollout plan
1) Internal beta: enable siphon for a handful of low-risk tenants and dev/test clusters; collect ledger correctness and latency data (4 weeks).
2) Soft enable: default off, opt-in for tenants via Console; gather UX feedback on pricing tooltips and visibility (6–8 weeks).
3) Guarded ramp: enable for small fraction of production traffic with hard caps and alert thresholds; measure impact on autoscaler triggers and neighbor SLOs (8–12 weeks).
4) General availability: expose billing lines and full Console controls; prepare partner comms.

Open questions & next work items
- Exact steadyback parameters: linear decay vs exponential? investigate both on synthetic workloads.
- M-credit unit sizing: should we peg to token slices, inference-call units, or cost equivalent? run pricing experiments.
- Interaction with Dedicated reservation rollups: if a tenant scales their reserved pool mid-epoch, how do we reconcile siphon ledger entries? (suggest make reconciliation idempotent on epoch boundary).
- UX for alerts: should tenant receive real-time notifications when siphon engages? (pro: transparency, con: noise).

Appendix: example scenarios
- Short demo spike (30s, +3x traffic): tenant consumes 20 M-credits, steadyback decays this over 15 minutes; billing shows single line item and console highlights spike. No neighbor impact; no autoscale.
- Sustained surge (20m): siphon hits threshold -> predictive autoscaler warms 2 extra slices; if surge persists autoscaler converts to committed reservation or tenant is recommended to purchase monthly commit.
- Abuse case: tenant with scripted high-frequency small calls -> siphon quickly exhausts, then requests hit hard throttle. Ops flag tenant for review.

Next steps (owner: Maya Lopez)
- Prototype siphon ledger events and router atomic check in infra sandbox (owner: Ethan Park) - 3w
- Pricing experiment model and placement in Console (owner: Priya Sharma) - 2w
- Synthetic workload tests for steadyback parameter sweep (owner: Liam OConnor) - 3w
- Draft API & Console wireframes (owner: Sofia Mendes) - 1w

Flags for PM review
- Need alignment on billing cadence and refund handling.
- Legal review required for explicit "siphon" purchase lines (consumer clarity).
- Security review for admin override capability.

References
- Slack thread: #prod-dedicated-scaling (see thread 2025-09-05)
- Confluence: RESERVE-MODEL-42 (linked above)
- Prototype PR: github.com/redwood-inference/dedicated-autoscaler/pull/314

Notes to self
- Keep naming concise in API (siphon vs micro-credit confusion).
- Consider short-lived coupons for early adopters to reduce churn risk.
